\title{Neither Memory nor an ODE-RNN: A Pre-Registered Negative Result\\
for Learned Adaptive-Therapy Policies under Burden-Only Observation}
\author{\name Anonymous \email anonymous@example.org \\ \addr Anonymous Institution}

\begin{document}
\maketitle

\begin{abstract}
In a virtual-patient simulator of adaptive cancer therapy, a memoryless network
that learns a one-line burden threshold matches or beats both a recurrent
network and an ODE-RNN trained by the same algorithm. Continuous-time recurrent
networks are proposed for control problems whose observations are irregular,
but they are mostly tested on prediction. We test one, the ODE-RNN, in a
pre-registered comparison: a policy doses a virtual tumour from noisy total
burden alone. One RL algorithm (PQN) trains a memoryless MLP, a
parameter-matched LSTM, an LSTM given the visit gap, and an ODE-RNN, compared
on paired virtual patients with confidence intervals over training seeds and
patients. The ODE-RNN never beats the best discrete arm: not in distribution,
not under a parameter shift, and not when up to half of the visits are missed
(one-year horizon). Giving the MLP only a clock costs as much as giving it
memory. The task is not solved: a per-patient search on the true simulator
beats the MLP by 23 days. Splitting a tuned threshold rule's gain, at most
${\sim}15$ days come from information that memory could supply, while
recurrent training costs 40--50. This is a negative result about this trainer
and this task: we do not show that no memory policy could help. We also report four
evaluation errors, each of which gave a wrong result that looked publishable,
and the five controls that found them.
\end{abstract}

\section{Introduction}
Adaptive therapy doses a tumour so that drug-sensitive cells stay alive and
compete with resistant cells, instead of trying to eradicate it. Reinforcement
learning (RL) has been used to schedule it. On a Lotka--Volterra (LV) model with
burden-only observation, A3C learns a treat-above-threshold rule close to the
clinical algorithm \cite{gallagher2024}, and recurrence has been reported to
help chemotherapy control when part of the state is hidden \cite{kiram2026}. A
natural next claim is that a policy whose hidden state is itself an ODE
\cite{rubanova2019} carries the right inductive bias. That bias should matter
most when the biology shifts or when visits are irregular. This is a general
question for RL under partial observation, and adaptive therapy is a small
test bed where we can check it against the true simulator.

We test that claim for one continuous-time design, the ODE-RNN, in a
pre-registered comparison, and it is not supported. The
main objection is that the recurrent arms were undertrained. We address it
partly without any trainer: a per-patient search on the true simulator shows
the task has headroom, and a tuned threshold rule's gain splits by the
information each part needs. At most ${\sim}15$ days of that gain need memory,
less than recurrent training cost. This is a split of one rule family's gain,
not a ceiling on every memory policy. Contributions:
\begin{itemize}
\item \textbf{A strict ablation.} One trainer, one environment and one
evaluation, with only the Q-network swapped; the recurrent arms are matched at
${\sim}3{,}100$ Q-path parameters.
\item \textbf{Negative results with seed+patient CIs}: no ODE-RNN edge in range
(Tier~0), under a parameter shift (Tier~1), or under missed visits (Tier~4), on
two parameter regimes and on models fitted to 55 patients. The best learned
policy is a burden threshold. A trainer-free full-information bound shows the
task has headroom and splits a threshold family's gain: at most ${\sim}15$ days
need memory-type information, while recurrent training cost 40--50.
\item \textbf{Four evaluation errors}, each of which gave a wrong result that
looked publishable, and the controls that found them
(\S\ref{sec:pitfalls}, Table~\ref{tab:controls}). Appendix material: monitoring
maps over cost of resistance, turnover and horizon (\S\ref{sec:monitoring}),
and a record of every registered run (Table~\ref{tab:runs}).
\end{itemize}

\section{Related work}
\paragraph{RL for adaptive therapy.} Learned dosing policies on tumour ODEs
have been reported to approach a clinical threshold rule from burden alone
\cite{gallagher2024}, to approach an optimal-control benchmark when every
subpopulation is observed \cite{kidane2026}, and to benefit from recurrence
when part of the state is hidden \cite{kiram2026}. None compares memory with
continuous time under one trainer, with seed-level uncertainty.
\paragraph{Memory in partially observed RL.} Carefully implemented recurrent
model-free RL is a strong POMDP baseline; there, as here, an oracle given the
hidden state under shared hyperparameters often scored below it
\cite{ni2022}. Across 13 memory models, classical RNNs beat modern ones and
a memoryless MLP is often not beaten at all \cite{morad2023}. Our MLP result
is this pattern in its extreme form; our headroom split (\S\ref{sec:results})
measures how little there was for memory to buy.
\paragraph{Continuous-time networks.} ODE-RNNs \cite{rubanova2019}, neural
CDEs \cite{kidger2020} and liquid time-constant networks \cite{hasani2021}
outperform discrete RNNs on irregularly sampled \emph{prediction}. Their
advantage is largest when the observation pattern itself is informative
\cite{rubanova2019,kidger2020}, and control is named as untested future work
\cite{hasani2021}. We test the control case, with gaps that carry no
information.

\section{Setup}
\paragraph{Virtual patients.} Sensitive cells $S$ and resistant cells $R$
compete for a shared capacity $K$:
\begin{align*}
\dot S &= r_S S\,(1 - \tfrac{S+R}{K})(1 - d_D u) - d_S S, &
\dot R &= r_R R\,(1 - \tfrac{S+R}{K}) - d_R R,
\end{align*}
with drug effect $u\in[0,1]$ from one-compartment PK. Patients are
Latin-hypercube samples of $\theta$ and of the initial resistant fraction $f_R$
and fill level $n_0$. The \emph{primary regime} follows Table~1 of Strobl et
al.\ \citeyearpar{strobl2021}: $r_S = 0.027\,\mathrm{d}^{-1}$, $r_R/r_S \in [0.5, 1]$,
one turnover $d_S=d_R=d_T$ with $d_T/r_S\in[0,0.5]$, $d_D=1.5$,
$n_0\in[0.1,0.75]$, $f_R\in[10^{-3},10^{-1}]$. Fed these parameters and
Strobl et al.'s two schedules, our implementation reproduces all 14 of their
published times to progression and adaptive-therapy gains that we checked,
within 3\% (their Fig.~4E and text). % R1, L871
A \emph{provisional regime}, on
which we first ran the study, has a much stronger cost of resistance (median
$r_R/r_S = 0.30$; only 9.8\% of its patients fall inside Strobl's sweep
ranges). Strobl et al.'s own fits to prostate-cancer patients extend to costs
above 50\%, paired with low turnover (their Fig.~5C). We therefore report it as
a second, high-cost regime, whose ranges are not taken from the literature.
% L703
\paragraph{Episodes and reward.} 52 weekly visits (357\,d). The policy sees
only $\log(\text{burden}/\text{baseline})$ with 5\% log-normal noise, never $S$
or $R$, and chooses a dose in $\{0, \tfrac12, 1\}$. Progression (TTP) is a 20\%
rise over the running nadir, confirmed over 28\,d. Training reward per visit is
$-\max(b/b_{\min}-1.2,\,0) - w\cdot\text{dose}$ (plus a constant), with
$w\in\{0.05,0.1,0.2,0.4\}$ as the exposure price. % erratum L739
\paragraph{Tiers.} The numbering follows a five-tier robustness plan; Tiers~2
(mechanism shift) and~3 (within-episode drift) are untested
(\S\ref{sec:limits}). Tier~0 uses the training ranges. Tier~1 scales $r_S, r_R$
by 1.5 and $K$ by 0.6, outside the training box. Tier~4 misses each visit with
probability $p$, i.i.d.; a missed visit gives no observation and no decision,
and the last dose continues (``hold'').
\paragraph{Arms.} MLP (width 441), LSTM (26 units), LSTM+$\Delta t$ (gap as a
second input, the standard discrete baseline for irregular series), a
positional MLP (width 386; memoryless, but also sees elapsed time, a standard
memory baseline \cite{morad2023}), and ODE-RNN
\cite{rubanova2019}. The ODE-RNN is a GRU jump at each observation, with a
tanh-bounded latent flow between observations in fixed $7/8$\,d steps, so gaps
of whole weeks compose exactly. All use a LayerNorm Q-readout, trained by PQN
\cite{gallici2024} with its published recurrent settings, untuned here, except
parallelism: 300 updates of 32 patients from a 200-patient training cohort,
where the paper uses 1024 environments (S3, in \S\ref{sec:results}, tests 1024).
\paragraph{Statistic.} Per patient, $U=\min(\mathrm{TTP},357)-w\cdot\text{exposure}$:
the TTP endpoint net of the exposure price the policy was trained with. Its
mean over patients is a restricted mean TTP net of exposure. The 357-d cap
bounds it, so no single patient can dominate it. Where the median of the paired
differences changes a reading, we say so.
$\Delta(A,B)$ is the mean over $w$ (and over $p\in\{0.2,0.5\}$ at Tier~4) of
the paired mean $U_A-U_B$ on 200 test patients. The 95\% CI comes from 2000
bootstrap resamples of \emph{training seeds and patients}. Every cell counts
(intention-to-treat); only non-finite rollouts would be excluded, and none
occurred. Beside $U$ we report capped median TTP with IQR, median exposure,
and the burden integral as a metastasis proxy. Reference rules: no treatment;
MTD, full dose throughout; AT50, the adaptive-therapy trial rule; thr0.8, full
dose above $0.8\times$ baseline.

\paragraph{Regular visits: memory hurts, continuous time adds nothing.} On
Strobl's ranges (Fig.~\ref{fig:forest}), ODE$-$MLP is \SAOdeMlpOne\ at Tier~1
and \SAOdeMlpZero\ at Tier~0, with all ten seeds negative. ODE$-$LSTM is
\SAOdeLstmOne, and LSTM$-$MLP \SAMemOne. Tier~0 and Tier~1 agree, so the gap is
a control deficit present without any shift, not a robustness effect. The
deficit is not specific to memory. A positional MLP, memoryless but given the
elapsed time, trails the MLP by as much ($-56.8$ [$-64.2$, $-48.3$] at Tier~1)
and ties the LSTM and ODE-RNN. The share of its doses explained by the current
observation halves (0.26 vs 0.48), to the ODE-RNN's 0.23. The deficit is a shortcut the trainer takes (Fig.~\ref{fig:shortcut}): trained with the clock hidden in
half of the episodes, the same network recovers it ($+54.4$ [$+44.9$, $+62.3$]
over the positional MLP at Tier~1) and ties the MLP ($-2.4$ [$-5.2$, $+0.4$]).
Scrambling the trained clock at test costs only $-14.6$ [$-44.2$, $+10.2$].
The same treatment does not help the recurrent arms: with their memory reset in
half of the training episodes, the LSTM and ODE-RNN gain $+4.3$ [$-13.1$, $+21.5$] and
$+4.2$ [$-8.8$, $+18.9$] at Tier~1 and stay $40$--$46$ days below the MLP. % V10 L1518
% V8 L1437, V9 L1477
Under missed visits it ties the MLP ($+2.2$ [$-13.2$, $+16.4$]). % V7 L1414
The
provisional regime gives the same ordering: LSTM$-$MLP \WCMemOne, ODE$-$LSTM
\WCOdeLstmOne\ (L596).

\begin{figure}[t]
\centering
\includegraphics[width=0.5\linewidth]{figures/fig_rule.pdf}
\caption{Mean greedy dose of the trained MLP policies against the observed
burden. The switch-on point sits near the thr0.8 rule. The step down above
${\sim}1.4\times$ baseline (Strobl ranges) lies where 99.9\% of visits are
already past progression, so a dose there only costs exposure.}
\label{fig:rule}
\end{figure}

\paragraph{The best learned policy is a threshold.} A memoryless MLP's dose is
a function of the current observation by construction. What matters is the
function's shape (Fig.~\ref{fig:rule}). On Strobl's ranges the mean dose crosses
one half at $\RuleHalfStrobl\times$ baseline and is full by $0.8\times$. The
one-line thr0.8 rule matches the MLP: mean $U$ \SAUMlpOne\ vs \SAUThrOne\ at
Tier~1, and \SAUMlpZero\ vs \SAUThrZero\ at Tier~0. With PQN's published
parallelism (below) the MLP is slightly above the rule, \SThreeUMlpZero\ vs
\SThreeUThrZero\ at Tier~0, by dosing less.

\paragraph{What memory could have bought.} At regular visits the simulator is
deterministic given the doses. The best policy with full information is
therefore the best dose sequence for each patient, and no trainer is needed to
bound it. A search on the true simulator, per test patient, beats the MLP by
$+23.1$ [$+20.3$, $+25.8$] days of $U$. A threshold rule whose level is tuned to
each patient does better still, $+26.0$ [$+23.5$, $+28.5$]: 14--19 more days to
progression on 46--60 fewer days of drug. So the task has room the MLP does not
reach. % O1, L1279
That room splits into three near-equal parts (Table~\ref{tab:split}). About a
third is a fixed, memoryless threshold near baseline, which the MLP could
represent but did not learn: the training reward charges for burden between the
nadir line and baseline. A second third is the value of observing the burden
exactly rather than with 5\% noise. That bounds what filtering the observation
history could recover. The last third is knowing each patient's best level,
which bounds what inferring the patient from history could add. For a threshold
policy, memory-type information is therefore worth at most ${\sim}15$ days.
This is a split of one rule family's gain, not a bound on memory: the search
(+23.1) is itself below the tuned threshold (+26.0), so it is not the
full-information optimum, and the first two rows of the table are post hoc.
Recurrent training cost 40--50. Read against the reference trainer failures
below, the negative result is a statement about PQN at this budget: a learning
cost larger than the benefit we can measure, not proof that memory has none.
% O1b, L1310
The recurrent arms also reach a lower training reward than the MLP on their
own training patients ($-20.7$ [$-28.4$, $-12.8$] and $-23.5$ [$-34.7$, $-14.0$]),
so they optimise the reward less well; they do not exploit it. % V1a, L1136
A reference trained like the arms but also shown $S$, $R$ and $\theta$ never
reached this headroom. It was \HFullZero\ below the MLP, then \SThreeFull\ at
PQN's published parallelism, and \TOneFull\ with ten times the gradient steps,
where it ties the MLP on training reward. That reward has no progression term.
Adding one (a survival term paid until confirmed progression) lifts the
reference by $+15.4$ [$+10.2$, $+20.8$] days and brings it level with the MLP
($-1.4$ [$-4.1$, $+1.2$]). It now wins on 62--69\% of patients (median $+2$ to
$+15$ days, mostly less drug) but its mean is lower because of a tail of earlier
progressions, so on the mean it recovers none of O1's $+23$ days. The reward
was part of the gap; the rest is PQN's difficulty in using the true state.
% S2 L804, S3 L840, T1 L1042, V2 L1344

\begin{figure}[t]
\centering
\includegraphics[width=\linewidth]{figures/fig_missed.pdf}
\caption{Mean $U$ over the four exposure prices against the share of visits
missed at test. All arms were trained with 35\% of visits missed; 10 seeds per

\label{fig:missed}

\paragraph{Missed visits: no continuous-time edge.} Trained with 35\% of
visits missed, the ODE-RNN is above none of its comparators on Strobl's ranges
(Fig.~\ref{fig:forest}): ODE$-$MLP \SBOdeMlp, $-$LSTM \SBOdeLstm,
$-$LSTM+$\Delta t$ \SBOdeLstmDt, $-$MTD \SBOdeMtd. It degrades more gracefully
than the MLP (\SBGraceMlp\ on $U(p)-U(0)$) but less than the LSTM
(\SBGraceLstm), so graceful degradation comes from recurrence, not from
continuous time. The ODE-RNN's one advantage over the MLP, at $p=0.5$, is an
exposure artefact: it doses more (median exposure 326 vs 194 at $w=0.1$), and
the comparison already nets that drug out in $U$. % L766
The provisional regime agrees: ODE$-$MLP \WBOdeMlp, ODE$-$MTD \WBOdeMtd.
One Tier-4 effect is unstable: adding $\Delta t$ to the LSTM changed $U$ by
$+38.8$, $+3.5$ and $-14.4$ in three independent runs, so we read LSTM+$\Delta t$
differences as seed noise.

\paragraph{Missed visits remove the value of feedback.} The MLP, best at regular
visits, loses most as visits go missing (Fig.~\ref{fig:missed}; mean $U$
\SBUMlpZero$\to$\SBUMlpHalf\ on Strobl's ranges, thr0.8
\SBUThrZero$\to$\SBUThrHalf). Under hold, a threshold policy that has switched
off keeps the drug off through the gap while the tumour regrows. At 20\% missed
the MLP is still above MTD (\SBUMlpFifth\ vs \SBUMtdFifth). At 50\%, no learned
policy is above MTD in either regime over our one-year horizon (but see
\S\ref{sec:monitoring} for three years). On Strobl's ranges the best arm (LSTM) ties it
(\SBFb); the MLP (\SBFbMlp) and LSTM+$\Delta t$ (\SBFbLstmDt) are below it,
and the ODE-RNN is at or below it (\SBFbOde). On the provisional ranges all four
arms are below it (best: \WBFbBest, \WBFb). These are statements about the
mean. For the median patient the LSTM beats MTD ($+10.7$ [$+1.7$, $+28.0$]):
about 45\% of patients are progression-free under both at one year, and the
LSTM uses less drug on them. Replayed unchanged over three years, every learned
arm beats MTD on $U$, by 32 to 82 days, but only the LSTM matches its time to
progression ($+9.0$ [$-9.4$, $+28.6$]\,d). The others progress earlier and win
on drug saved, as the threshold rules do (\S\ref{sec:monitoring}). The
ODE-RNN shows no edge there either (ODE$-$LSTM $-32.1$ [$-70.9$, $+9.1$]).
% V1b, V1c, L1136

\paragraph{Models fitted to patients; monitoring maps.} Replaying the saved
policies on models fitted to 55 prostate-cancer patients, both negatives
replicate (Appendix~\ref{sec:fitted}). Whether feedback survives missed visits
need not depend on architecture at all: with threshold rules only, it stops
beating MTD at 10--50\% missed visits over one year, and the crossover depends
on cost of resistance, turnover and horizon (Appendix~\ref{sec:monitoring}).

\section{Four evaluation errors}\label{sec:pitfalls}
\begin{enumerate}
\item \textbf{Open-loop collapse.} Under PPO, the ODE-RNN gave all 200 patients
one identical exposure in 4 of 6 cells. Our first ``architecture'' result
thus compared feedback with a fixed schedule (L312). The cause was
initialisation: each 7-day flow drove the hidden state to a saturated fixed
point, and an untrained policy's entropy fell from 1.07 to 0 within one
episode (L353).
\item \textbf{The collapse gate becomes wrong under missed visits.} Once
observations were unreliable, near-fixed schedules scored \emph{higher} than
closed-loop cells, so excluding them biased the comparison (L632). We moved to
intention-to-treat, with MTD as a reference arm to beat.
\item \textbf{Training instability looks like an architecture effect.} A
$2\times10^{-7}$ change in a float moved one ODE-RNN cell's mean $U$ from 132
to 256\,d. Patient-only CIs ($[-20,-11]$) showed the ODE-RNN worse than the
LSTM; resampling seeds widened them to $[-43,+22]$ (L596).
\item \textbf{A mis-built shifted cohort.} Shifting $K$ after computing $y_0$
put 43--50\% of Tier-1 patients above capacity. Under full dose 14--18\% of
them diverged to NaN, and these were scored as censored, i.e.\ as successes
(L242). A progressor-only TTP median and TTP bought with extra drug misled us
in similar ways. This is why every comparison here uses the censoring-aware estimator and the
exposure term.
\end{enumerate}

\begin{table}[t]
\centering\footnotesize
\caption{Controls for claims about memory or continuous time in partially
observed RL: what each catches here, and its cost.}
\label{tab:controls}
\resizebox{\linewidth}{!}{\begin{tabular}{@{}p{0.34\linewidth}p{0.40\linewidth}p{0.22\linewidth}@{}}
\toprule
Control & Error it catches here & Cost \\
\midrule
Memoryless and clock-only baselines & ``Memory helps'' when a threshold does as well; a clock costs as much as memory (V7) & two extra arms \\
Trainer-free headroom bound, split by information & ``Undertrained recurrent nets'': memory could buy $\le 15$\,d (O1b) & one search on the simulator \\
CIs over training seeds and test cases & A patient-only CI that held trained policies fixed (item 3) & $\ge 5$ seeds per arm \\
Policy cost next to its score & TTP bought with drug; progressor-only medians (item 4) & one exposure term \\
Failed runs kept in the count & A validity gate that selected the better cells (item 2); open-loop collapse (item 1) & intention-to-treat reporting \\
\bottomrule
\end{tabular}}
\end{table}



\section{Limitations}\label{sec:limits}
One ODE family (LV), virtual patients only, and no claim about clinical
outcomes. PQN's settings are the published ones except parallelism (32 patients
per update, not 1024) and untuned, and the recurrent arms are unstable in
training; we treat that as part of their cost rather than tuning it away. Given
the true hidden state, PQN at the registered budgets scores below the
burden-only MLP. With ten times the gradient steps it matches the MLP on the
training reward and still trails on $U$, and with a progression term in the reward it
ties the MLP on mean $U$. Neither change opened the registered 10-day gate, so
we stopped the reward and budget search there, instead of tuning until it passed.
We test one continuous-time design, the ODE-RNN; liquid time-constant
\cite{hasani2021} and neural-CDE \cite{kidger2020} arms are untested. Missed visits are i.i.d., so the next gap is unknown when the policy doses.
On a fixed visit schedule with the time to the next visit given as an input,
the ODE-RNN is below the MLP on held-out schedules ($-21.4$ [$-42.8$, $-2.9$]);
trained on a pool of schedules it is above the MLP ($+34.8$ [$+16.1$, $+53.7$]),
but so is the LSTM, and the MLP never gains from the input ($+1.4$ [$-10.3$,
$+14.4$]), so neither run tests whether a known schedule helps a continuous-time
state. % W8 L1457, W9 L1498
Before
testing mechanism shift (Tier~2) we checked three other tumour models.
Kuznetsov has no resistant population, so MTD is optimal by construction;
Hahnfeldt is a mouse model with no resistant population, which our
implementation reproduces in its own units except for two narrow misses
\cite{hahnfeldt1999}; and the
three-population model behind the clinical adaptive-therapy trial
\cite{zhang2017} reproduces structurally (22/22 equilibria) but not in its
published progression times (at most 15/40). % W5-pre L1004, V5 L1176, V5e L1248
LV is the only family here with a resistance mechanism, so
every result is LV-only. Within LV, the negatives hold on two parameter regimes,
under a parameter shift, and on models fitted to 55 patients, and our
implementation reproduces Strobl et al.'s published times to progression.
Within-episode drift (Tier~3) is untested. The learned
policies were compared over one year only. The monitoring maps show that the
absolute value of feedback under missed visits depends on the horizon, so
``no learned policy beats MTD at 50\% missed'' is a one-year statement about the
mean. The maps
cover threshold rules only; over one year at low turnover the best rule sits
at the grid's most aggressive level. $U$ is a mean. On medians the three-year
win holds only where resistance is nearly free, and the sparing rules always
carry a larger tumour burden, which our metastasis proxy counts against them.

\section{Conclusion}\label{sec:conclusion}
On this task a memoryless burden threshold is a strong baseline, and neither
memory nor continuous time beat it, on two parameter regimes and on models
fitted to 55 patients' PSA. The task has headroom, but most of it is a better
threshold or better measurement, not something a recurrent state could infer;
what memory could add (${\sim}15$ days) is smaller than what recurrent training
cost (40--50). Even given the hidden state, and with a reward that pays until
progression, the same trainer only ties the burden-only MLP. When half of the
visits are missed, the question is no longer which architecture uses feedback
best but whether feedback has any value; over one year, on average, it had none.
A continuous-time policy needs a setting where the gap itself carries
information, such as scheduled rather than random visits, and a trainer that
can first beat the threshold with the true state.

\paragraph{Controls for similar claims.} Before reporting an architecture
effect in partially observed RL, we suggest the five controls of
Table~\ref{tab:controls}.

\section{Models fitted to patients}\label{sec:fitted}
Strobl et al.\ fitted this model to
PSA from \RTwoN\ men in an intermittent androgen-suppression trial
\cite{strobl2021}. We repeated their fit with our simulator: \RTwoExcl\ fits
fail their $r^2 \ge 0.5$ rule (theirs: 15), and fitted cost and turnover are
anticorrelated (\RTwoPearson; theirs $-0.77$). Their relapse separation holds in
direction only ($p = \RTwoMWp$, post hoc after a mis-registered test). Replaying
the saved policies, unchanged, on the \POneN\ kept fits: at regular visits
ODE-RNN$-$MLP is \POneOdeMlp\ and ODE-RNN$-$LSTM \POneOdeLstm; with half the
visits missed, no learned arm beats MTD (ODE-RNN \POneOdeMtd, LSTM
\POneLstmMtd). MTD keeps every fitted patient progression-free for a year, so
this replay tests drug use more than progression time. These are models fitted
to patients, not patients. % R2 L1075, P1 L1106

\section{When does monitoring stop being useful?}\label{sec:monitoring}
Whether feedback survives missed visits need not depend on architecture at all.
We binned patients by cost of resistance ($r_R/r_S$) and turnover ($d_T/r_S$).
In each bin we compared the best burden-threshold rule with MTD, with rules
only and no learning (Fig.~\ref{fig:monitoring}; pre-registered). The rule's
level is chosen on a selection cohort and scored on test patients. With
reliable monitoring, feedback beats MTD in every bin, by \MOneRegMin\ to
\MOneRegMax\ days over one year. The share of missed visits at which it stops
doing so rises as resistance becomes cheaper: from \MOnePStarLowMin\ to
\MOnePStarLowMax\ at low turnover, and from \MOnePStarHighMin\ to
\MOnePStarHighMax\ at high turnover. At 50\% missed, the costliest bin inside
Strobl's sweep trails the no-cost end by \MOneCostLow\ days at low turnover
and \MOneCostHigh\ at high turnover. Feedback thus tolerates unreliable
monitoring best where adaptive therapy helps most \cite{strobl2021}. % M1, L896

\paragraph{The horizon changes the answer.} Over one year, MTD reaches the end of
the horizon for most patients in the costliest bins, so we followed the same
patients for three years (Fig.~\ref{fig:monitoring}, bottom). The cost effect
survives: \MOneBCostLow\ and \MOneBCostHigh\ days at 50\% missed. The crossover
moves later, to \MOneBPStarLowMin--\MOneBPStarLowMax\ at low turnover and
\MOneBPStarHigh\ at high turnover. There, sparing thresholds beat MTD by
\MOneBHighMin\ to \MOneBHighMax\ days at 50\% missed. Within three years MTD
fails in nearly every patient inside Strobl's range, while sparing dosing holds
a minority for the whole horizon. At the no-cost end, \MOneBTailCens\ of
patients never progress under the threshold rule, which uses \MOneBExpCut\ less
drug. Its \emph{median} TTP is nonetheless shorter than MTD's (\MOneBMedThr\ vs
\MOneBMedMtd\ days): the gain is a heavy right tail plus drug saved, which $U$
rewards and the median does not. Dosing through missed visits, which helped
over one year (\MOneMiss), now helps at low turnover but hurts at high turnover
(pooled \MOneBMiss). % M1b, L932

\paragraph{Medians narrow the claim.} $U$ above is a mean over patients. Scored
on medians instead (a post-hoc analysis of the same runs, with the threshold
also chosen by median), the three-year gain at high turnover and 50\% missed
survives only in the two lowest-cost bins, $\hat r_R \ge 0.75$ (\MOneCHighThree\
and \MOneCHighFour\ days). In the two costliest bins inside Strobl's sweep it
reverses (\MOneCHighOne\ and \MOneCHighTwo). The cost effect holds under medians
over three years but not over one year at low turnover (\MOneCCostOneLow). In
all 20 bin$\times$horizon cells at 50\% missed, the selected threshold rule has
a shorter median TTP and a larger median burden integral than MTD (by
\MOneCBurdenNoCost\ at the three-year no-cost end, $\MOneCBurdenCostly\times$ in
the costliest Strobl bin). Where sparing wins for the median patient, it wins
on drug saved, not on time bought or tumour held down. % M1c, L968

\begin{table}[h]

\caption{Settings shared by every arm. PQN values are the published recurrent
settings \cite{gallici2024}, untuned, except parallelism.}
\label{tab:hparams}

\toprule
Trainer & PQN, Peng's Q($\lambda$), no replay, no target network \\
Learning rate & $3\times10^{-4}$, linear decay to 0 \\
$\gamma$, $\lambda$ & 0.99, 0.5 \\
Epochs $\times$ minibatches & $4\times4$, minibatches of whole patient episodes \\
$\varepsilon$-greedy & $1.0\to0.005$ over the first 10\% of updates \\
Max gradient norm & 0.5 \\

Reward scale & 0.01 \\
\midrule
MLP & one hidden layer, width 441, LayerNorm \\

ODE-RNN & GRU jump, 16-d latent, field width 64, fixed $7/8$\,d steps \\
\midrule
PK & bolus, clearance $0.5\,\mathrm{d}^{-1}$, $E_{\max}$ effect, $EC_{50}=0.5$ \\

Everything is written in JAX, Equinox and Diffrax and runs on CPU (one Intel
i7-13800H); rollouts use fixed-step solvers, which we found accurate to
${\sim}10^{-4}$ and faster than adaptive stepping or GPU at this batch size.
The largest single run (V2, 80 cells at 1024 patients and 3000 updates) took
about 150 CPU-hours. Code, pre-registrations and the dated research log
referenced in Table~\ref{tab:runs} will be released with the paper.
